reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This manuscript from the Jacob’s laboratory characterizes the tsk mutant in Arabidopsis thaliana and reveals the rapid accumulation of large Tandem Duplications (TD) in this mutant, provoking in few generations an increase of more than 6% of the genome size. They demonstrate that the TD arose independently, are inherited in a mendelian fashion and possess specific signatures consistent with TMEJ.

Importantly, the original data presented, as well as the reanalyze of previously published data allowed the authors to confirm the existence of a molecular pathways required to maintain genome stability at replication forks by preventing tandem duplications via the DDR, and composed of several mutants confirm CAF-1, H3.1, TSK and TOP1α.

The data presented are well described, robust and the conclusions appropriate. Ultimately, the information revealed in this paper provides important insights into understanding the emergence of these tandem duplications. The fact that they are revealed in an in-planta system does not detract from their importance, especially in a context where studying this pathway is particularly complex in mammals due to the lethality induced by mutations in the actors involved in this pathway.

I only have one main comment :
The authors analysed whether TD accumulation was linked to specific chromatic states in Figure 3C, but they did not specifically and individually analyse the different chromatic modifications and histone variants enriched in these regions. However, their systematic analyses could reveal the presence of a specific modification. Furthermore, previous observations of induced TD boundaries (reference #23 in this MS) corresponded to the boundaries of topologically associated domains (TADs). Given that more than 200 TDs were identified in tsk-4 lines, I am curious to see whether they are enriched within TAD boundaries or in the transition between compartments A and B.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Thomson et al. examine the role of the TONSL (plant TSK) complex in the formation of genomic tandem duplications resulting from replication stress in Arabidopsis. TSK loss increases duplication occurrence and genetically interacts with DNA Pol theta (POLQ) deficiency. Presumed checkpoint activation in response to DNA damage in tsk mutant plants leads to developmental phenotypes.

Tandem duplications are an interesting and important subclass of genomic alterations in cancer, agriculture, and evolution and their mechanisms are poorly understood. The current work is highly valuable as the impact of TONSL loss of function on mammalian cell genomic instability has been harder to study due to lethality. The paper is well written and clear, and figures are well drawn and easy to understand, except for minor concerns below.

The specific and substantial induction of relatively large tandem duplications in plant genomes, and their accumulation across generations and within somatic tissues, is clear and striking from WGS data. The data from other plants with alterations in related genes is supportive. In total, the most important observation in the paper – increased tandem duplication occurrence resulting from TSK loss – is solid and the strength of the paper.

The limitation is that the study is largely phenomenological with few observations that clearly reveal mechanistic insight. In this regard, I am not especially compelled by the genome enrichment analyses that are likely underpowered, the checkpoint studies address the organism-level growth defect more than the genomic events and are not terribly surprising, and even the POLQ studies don’t fully arrive at establishing the unique role of TMEJ in duplication junction formation (although that is entirely plausible and most consistent with the data). However, nothing in the paper tells us much about why TONSL and its partners lead to the unique duplication phenotype, which is the striking finding of the study, as opposed to other outcomes, what role chromatin or recombination plays, etc.

Major additional comments:
1) It is unclear why tsk teb (polq) double mutants are synthetic lethal. Even if the observed tandem duplications are POLQ-mediated, is the lesion burden high enough to lead to lethality, especially in the face of other DSB repair pathways? Cellular studies could help explore these issues by separating cell autonomous and organismal defects.
2) Regardless of the reason, the synthetic lethality makes it tough to fully conclude that the tandem duplications are POLQ-mediated. I very much agree with the importance and interpretation of the junction properties, especially the templated insertions. But some conclusions around POLQ are likely overstated since the double mutant phenotype does not actually show a reduction, or change in the properties, of CNVs when POLQ is absent, it shows synthetic lethality for reasons that are not established by the data provided.
3) When performing enrichment analysis by simulation, it is important that simulated events are only allowed to occur in locations that could have been detected in short sequencing reads that fell in that location; poorly mappable regions of the genome should be excluded. Otherwise, enrichment effects can be dominated by sequencing bias (more of a problem in the plant genome? I am not expert on that point). The methods do not indicate that such effects were considered, since simulated CNVs (unlike real CNVs) were allowed to fall anywhere in the genome as it is written. A secondary strategy can examine whether total aligned reads/read coverage show an enrichment bias relative to scored genomic spans.
4) Regarding data sufficiency, there are a relatively small number of plants per group, but in most cases this seems sufficient since tsk mutant effects are large per individual, especially after multiple mutant generations. However, the number of plants sequenced of course correlates to the number of duplication events observed. Here, 481 events is decent but not overly powerful at detecting genomic feature enrichment, unless effects are large. The enrichment analysis in Figure 3 is hampered by relatively low total event numbers leading to suggestive trends that could be made more compelling. Given the large size of the duplications, it would seem plausible to sequence more plants at low coverage (and thus similar net cost). The stated coverage in Table S4 is quite high, often exceeding 100-fold (I assume “coverage” means “fold genome coverage”). Large duplications can be detected with a lot less read density than that, more than 10-fold less (the authors could explore for themselves how much coverage they would need per plant by downsampling current data). I would welcome the accumulation of many more events to power the genomic analysis. That said, I understand it may not be the best use of resources, since genomic location is probably not the thing that drives the most critical mechanistic questions in any case.

A few minor comments about figures:
5) I like the CNV size plots stratified by sequenced plant, but the plots can be hard to interpret since the number of plotted events can be difficult to discern. I suggest putting the event number on the plots. Also, on these plots, is it possible (was it done?) to isolate duplications that arose in that individual separately from those in the parental lineage? I understand that information may not always be available in the absence of multi-generational studies.
6) It’s a small detail, but I don’t think the authors should use the same red and green coloring for the traces and the arrows in figures like Fig. 3F. I don’t think they intend for the arrow colors to match the trace colors.
7) I especially like Fig. 5A, which does an excellent job placing the current observations in the context of tandem duplications in human cancer.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In this manuscript, the authors reported that the tsk mutants rapidly accumulate large, heritable tandem duplications, which may be mediated by Pol θ. They also found that mutations in WEE1 and SOG1 partially rescued the developmental defects of tsk. The possible role of TSK in the formation of tandem duplications is very interesting. But the underlying mechanism is not well explored. More evidence is needed to further support their conclusions.

1. The authors concluded that the tandem duplications in the tsk mutant were attributed to Pol θ, which was supported by the mutational signatures of the tandem duplications. Since this is one of the major findings of the manuscript, the genetic evidence is needed to further support it. As the tsk-4 teb-5 double mutant was lethal, the authors may consider to use the weak teb allele teb-3 (SALK_001669) or knock down TEB using RNAi. The lethality of tsk-4 teb-5 actually suggests that TSK and TEB can function independently. Given that the authors found that c-NHEJ was not responsible for the tandem duplications in tsk-4 mutants, it is possible that the HR pathway may be involved in this process. Therefore, it is worthwhile to cross tsk-4 with HR mutants such as brca1 and rad51 and test the phenotype of the double mutant.
2. They performed reciprocal crosses between the tsk-4 mutant and Col-0 and concluded that the developmental phenotypes of tsk-4 plants are associated with the absence of TSK rather than the presence of tandem duplications within the genome. But the evidence to support this conclusion is not strong. Based on Figure 4B, compared with TSK +/+ plants, many more TSK +/- plants showed a high percentage of nodes with double siliques (>25%), especially in tsk-4 x Col-0. The statistical insignificance of the difference between TSK +/- and TSK -/- may be due to the small sample size. It is still possible that the tandem duplications cause the developmental phenotypes. Therefore, on the one hand, the authors need to increase the sample size. On the other hand, the authors need to examine the number of tandem duplications in TSK +/+, TSK +/-, and TSK -/- in the segregating population.
3. It was very interesting that wee1 and sog1 partially suppressed the developmental phenotypes of tsk-4. The authors mentioned that“The inability to repair damaged DNA in the absence of TSK is a source of cellular stress”(line 270). Given that WEE1 and SOG1 positively regulate DNA repair, it is likely that tsk wee1 and tsk sog1 accumulate more DNA damage, which needs to be tested. Alternatively, the phenotypes of tsk-4 are not due to DNA damage per se but due to the activation of DDR, which is suppressed when WEE1 or SOG1 is mutated. WEE1 and SOG1 are known to function downstream of ATR. Given the difference of wee1 and sog1 in suppressing tsk-4, it will be interesting to test whether atr can suppress tsk-4 better than wee1 and sog1.
4. In the title, the authors concluded that tandem duplications are induced by replication stress. Although TSK is proposed to regulate DNA replication, whether replication stress indeed induces tandem duplications is not clear. Some unknown factors may account for the enhanced tandem duplications in tsk-4. If the authors want to conclude that tandem duplications are induced by replication stress, they may examine tandem duplications in Col-0 and tsk-4 treated by replication stress-inducing chemicals such as hydroxyurea.
5. Statistical analysis is needed for Figures 2B, 2C, 2G, and 4D to test whether the difference is significant or not.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We want to thank the reviewers for the comments provided on our initial manuscript. A point-by-point response to all comments is provided below.

We have also added new data in the revised manuscript that was not suggested by the reviewers, but that we believe is very important to our study based on questions we received when presenting this work. These experiments were initiated last summer and provided results after the initial submission of our manuscript to Nature Communications.

In the course of this study, we came to the conclusion that the copy number variations (CNVs) we were observing in tsk-4 mutant plants were tandem duplications. This was on account of chimeric short (150bp) reads being found linking the beginning and end of the CNV indicative of a breakpoint junction. Additionally, as shown in Figure S1E, these CNVs occurred at levels 1.5-2x the genomic DNA content of the wild type, suggesting a doubling of DNA.

However, mammalian cells experiencing various forms of genome instability have been shown to produce circular extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA), which are structures not integrated into chromosomes. Importantly, such structures are indistinguishable from tandem duplications in high-throughput short-read sequencing data. Therefore, there was a possibility that the CNVs identified in our study could be circular ecDNA.

Confirming a tandem duplication requires the identification of long DNA molecules that span the amplification itself and both junctions between amplified and non-amplified genomic DNA. To do this, we have now performed Optical Genome Mapping of a sample of pooled tsk-4 sibling plants and compared the resulting DNA molecules to 11 CNVs observed in the parent plant. We observed DNA molecules covering both copies of the duplication as well as flanking sequences for all CNVs up to 178 kb in size (6 CNVs), thus demonstrating that they are tandem duplications. While definitive results for the remaining larger CNVs were limited by the technical constraints of the assay, long DNA molecules consistent with tandem duplications were also found for all the remaining CNVs. Together, this new data confirms the conclusion that we are observing tandem duplications integrated into the chromosome of tsk-4 plants and not ecDNA. We included this data in the revised manuscript in Fig. 2.

As can be seen in the graph to the right (left panel), the intersection of breakends (+/- 50bp) with regions of poor mappability is within the bounds of what would be expected by chance, suggesting that the precision of breakend mapping is not impaired. ### Reviewer 1

This manuscript from the Jacob’s laboratory characterizes the tsk mutant in Arabidopsis thaliana and reveals the rapid accumulation of large Tandem Duplications (TD) in this mutant, provoking in few generations an increase of more than 6% of the genome size. They demonstrate that the TD arose independently, are inherited in a mendelian fashion and possess specific signatures consistent with TMEJ.

Importantly, the original data presented, as well as the reanalyze of previously published data allowed the authors to confirm the existence of a molecular pathways required to maintain genome stability at replication forks by preventing tandem duplications via the DDR, and composed of several mutants confirm CAF-1, H3.1, TSK and TOP1α.

The data presented are well described, robust and the conclusions appropriate. Ultimately, the information revealed in this paper provides important insights into understanding the emergence of these tandem duplications. The fact that they are revealed in an in-planta system does not detract from their importance, especially in a context where studying this pathway is particularly complex in mammals due to the lethality induced by mutations in the actors involved in this pathway.

I only have one main comment :
The authors analysed whether TD accumulation was linked to specific chromatic states in Figure 3C, but they did not specifically and individually analyse the different chromatic modifications and histone variants enriched in these regions. However, their systematic analyses could reveal the presence of a specific modification. Furthermore, previous observations of induced TD boundaries (reference #23 in this MS) corresponded to the boundaries of topologically associated domains (TADs). Given that more than 200 TDs were identified in tsk-4 lines, I am curious to see whether they are enriched within TAD boundaries or in the transition between compartments A and B.

### Reviewer 2

Thomson et al. examine the role of the TONSL (plant TSK) complex in the formation of genomic tandem duplications resulting from replication stress in Arabidopsis. TSK loss increases duplication occurrence and genetically interacts with DNA Pol theta (POLQ) deficiency. Presumed checkpoint activation in response to DNA damage in tsk mutant plants leads to developmental phenotypes.

Tandem duplications are an interesting and important subclass of genomic alterations in cancer, agriculture, and evolution and their mechanisms are poorly understood. The current work is highly valuable as the impact of TONSL loss of function on mammalian cell genomic instability has been harder to study due to lethality. The paper is well written and clear, and figures are well drawn and easy to understand, except for minor concerns below.

The specific and substantial induction of relatively large tandem duplications in plant genomes, and their accumulation across generations and within somatic tissues, is clear and striking from WGS data. The data from other plants with alterations in related genes is supportive. In total, the most important observation in the paper – increased tandem duplication occurrence resulting from TSK loss – is solid and the strength of the paper.

The limitation is that the study is largely phenomenological with few observations that clearly reveal mechanistic insight. In this regard, I am not especially compelled by the genome enrichment analyses that are likely underpowered, the checkpoint studies address the organism-level growth defect more than the genomic events and are not terribly surprising, and even the POLQ studies don’t fully arrive at establishing the unique role of TMEJ in duplication junction formation (although that is entirely plausible and most consistent with the data). However, nothing in the paper tells us much about why TONSL and its partners lead to the unique duplication phenotype, which is the striking finding of the study, as opposed to other outcomes, what role chromatin or recombination plays, etc.

Major additional comments:
1) It is unclear why tsk teb (polq) double mutants are synthetic lethal. Even if the observed tandem duplications are POLQ-mediated, is the lesion burden high enough to lead to lethality, especially in the face of other DSB repair pathways? Cellular studies could help explore these issues by separating cell autonomous and organismal defects.
2) Regardless of the reason, the synthetic lethality makes it tough to fully conclude that the tandem duplications are POLQ-mediated. I very much agree with the importance and interpretation of the junction properties, especially the templated insertions. But some conclusions around POLQ are likely overstated since the double mutant phenotype does not actually show a reduction, or change in the properties, of CNVs when POLQ is absent, it shows synthetic lethality for reasons that are not established by the data provided.
3) When performing enrichment analysis by simulation, it is important that simulated events are only allowed to occur in locations that could have been detected in short sequencing reads that fell in that location; poorly mappable regions of the genome should be excluded. Otherwise, enrichment effects can be dominated by sequencing bias (more of a problem in the plant genome? I am not expert on that point). The methods do not indicate that such effects were considered, since simulated CNVs (unlike real CNVs) were allowed to fall anywhere in the genome as it is written. ### Reviewer 3

In this manuscript, the authors reported that the tsk mutants rapidly accumulate large, heritable tandem duplications, which may be mediated by Pol θ. They also found that mutations in WEE1 and SOG1 partially rescued the developmental defects of tsk. The possible role of TSK in the formation of tandem duplications is very interesting. Given that the authors found that c-NHEJ was not responsible for the tandem duplications in tsk-4 mutants, it is possible that the HR pathway may be involved in this process. Therefore, it is worthwhile to cross tsk-4 with HR mutants such as brca1 and rad51 and test the phenotype of the double mutant.
2. They performed reciprocal crosses between the tsk-4 mutant and Col-0 and concluded that the developmental phenotypes of tsk-4 plants are associated with the absence of TSK rather than the presence of tandem duplications within the genome. The statistical insignificance of the difference between TSK +/- and TSK -/- may be due to the small sample size. It is still possible that the tandem duplications cause the developmental phenotypes. Therefore, on the one hand, the authors need to increase the sample size. On the other hand, the authors need to examine the number of tandem duplications in TSK +/+, TSK +/-, and TSK -/- in the segregating population.
3. It was very interesting that wee1 and sog1 partially suppressed the developmental phenotypes of tsk-4. The authors mentioned that“The inability to repair damaged DNA in the absence of TSK is a source of cellular stress”(line 270). Given that WEE1 and SOG1 positively regulate DNA repair, it is likely that tsk wee1 and tsk sog1 accumulate more DNA damage, which needs to be tested. Alternatively, the phenotypes of tsk-4 are not due to DNA damage per se but due to the activation of DDR, which is suppressed when WEE1 or SOG1 is mutated. WEE1 and SOG1 are known to function downstream of ATR. Given the difference of wee1 and sog1 in suppressing tsk-4, it will be interesting to test whether atr can suppress tsk-4 better than wee1 and sog1.
4. In the title, the authors concluded that tandem duplications are induced by replication stress. Although TSK is proposed to regulate DNA replication, whether replication stress indeed induces tandem duplications is not clear. Some unknown factors may account for the enhanced tandem duplications in tsk-4. If the authors want to conclude that tandem duplications are induced by replication stress, they may examine tandem duplications in Col-0 and tsk-4 treated by replication stress-inducing chemicals such as hydroxyurea.
5. Statistical analysis is needed for Figures 2B, 2C, 2G, and 4D to test whether the difference is significant or not.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript from the Jacob’s laboratory characterizes the tsk mutant in Arabidopsis thaliana and reveals the rapid accumulation of large Tandem Duplications (TD) in this mutant, provoking in few generations an increase of more than 6% of the genome size. They demonstrate that the TD arose independently, are inherited in a mendelian fashion and possess specific signatures consistent with TMEJ.

Importantly, the original data presented, as well as the reanalyze of previously published data allowed the authors to confirm the existence of a molecular pathways required to maintain genome stability at replication forks by preventing tandem duplications via the DDR, and composed of several mutants confirm CAF-1, H3.1, TSK and TOP1α.

The data presented are well described, robust and the conclusions appropriate. Ultimately, the information revealed in this paper provides important insights into understanding the emergence of these tandem duplications. The fact that they are revealed in an in-planta system does not detract from their importance, especially in a context where studying this pathway is particularly complex in mammals due to the lethality induced by mutations in the actors involved in this pathway.

I only have one main comment :
The authors analysed whether TD accumulation was linked to specific chromatic states in Figure 3C, but they did not specifically and individually analyse the different chromatic modifications and histone variants enriched in these regions. However, their systematic analyses could reveal the presence of a specific modification. Furthermore, previous observations of induced TD boundaries (reference #23 in this MS) corresponded to the boundaries of topologically associated domains (TADs). Given that more than 200 TDs were identified in tsk-4 lines, I am curious to see whether they are enriched within TAD boundaries or in the transition between compartments A and B.

### Reviewer 2

Thomson et al. examine the role of the TONSL (plant TSK) complex in the formation of genomic tandem duplications resulting from replication stress in Arabidopsis. TSK loss increases duplication occurrence and genetically interacts with DNA Pol theta (POLQ) deficiency. Presumed checkpoint activation in response to DNA damage in tsk mutant plants leads to developmental phenotypes.

Tandem duplications are an interesting and important subclass of genomic alterations in cancer, agriculture, and evolution and their mechanisms are poorly understood. The current work is highly valuable as the impact of TONSL loss of function on mammalian cell genomic instability has been harder to study due to lethality. The paper is well written and clear, and figures are well drawn and easy to understand, except for minor concerns below.

The specific and substantial induction of relatively large tandem duplications in plant genomes, and their accumulation across generations and within somatic tissues, is clear and striking from WGS data. The data from other plants with alterations in related genes is supportive. In total, the most important observation in the paper – increased tandem duplication occurrence resulting from TSK loss – is solid and the strength of the paper.

The limitation is that the study is largely phenomenological with few observations that clearly reveal mechanistic insight. In this regard, I am not especially compelled by the genome enrichment analyses that are likely underpowered, the checkpoint studies address the organism-level growth defect more than the genomic events and are not terribly surprising, and even the POLQ studies don’t fully arrive at establishing the unique role of TMEJ in duplication junction formation (although that is entirely plausible and most consistent with the data). However, nothing in the paper tells us much about why TONSL and its partners lead to the unique duplication phenotype, which is the striking finding of the study, as opposed to other outcomes, what role chromatin or recombination plays, etc.

Major additional comments:
1) It is unclear why tsk teb (polq) double mutants are synthetic lethal. Even if the observed tandem duplications are POLQ-mediated, is the lesion burden high enough to lead to lethality, especially in the face of other DSB repair pathways? Cellular studies could help explore these issues by separating cell autonomous and organismal defects.
2) Regardless of the reason, the synthetic lethality makes it tough to fully conclude that the tandem duplications are POLQ-mediated. I very much agree with the importance and interpretation of the junction properties, especially the templated insertions. But some conclusions around POLQ are likely overstated since the double mutant phenotype does not actually show a reduction, or change in the properties, of CNVs when POLQ is absent, it shows synthetic lethality for reasons that are not established by the data provided.
3) When performing enrichment analysis by simulation, it is important that simulated events are only allowed to occur in locations that could have been detected in short sequencing reads that fell in that location; poorly mappable regions of the genome should be excluded. Otherwise, enrichment effects can be dominated by sequencing bias (more of a problem in the plant genome? I am not expert on that point). The methods do not indicate that such effects were considered, since simulated CNVs (unlike real CNVs) were allowed to fall anywhere in the genome as it is written. A secondary strategy can examine whether total aligned reads/read coverage show an enrichment bias relative to scored genomic spans.
4) Regarding data sufficiency, there are a relatively small number of plants per group, but in most cases this seems sufficient since tsk mutant effects are large per individual, especially after multiple mutant generations. However, the number of plants sequenced of course correlates to the number of duplication events observed. Here, 481 events is decent but not overly powerful at detecting genomic feature enrichment, unless effects are large. The enrichment analysis in Figure 3 is hampered by relatively low total event numbers leading to suggestive trends that could be made more compelling. Given the large size of the duplications, it would seem plausible to sequence more plants at low coverage (and thus similar net cost). The stated coverage in Table S4 is quite high, often exceeding 100-fold (I assume “coverage” means “fold genome coverage”). Large duplications can be detected with a lot less read density than that, more than 10-fold less (the authors could explore for themselves how much coverage they would need per plant by downsampling current data). I would welcome the accumulation of many more events to power the genomic analysis. That said, I understand it may not be the best use of resources, since genomic location is probably not the thing that drives the most critical mechanistic questions in any case.

A few minor comments about figures:
5) I like the CNV size plots stratified by sequenced plant, but the plots can be hard to interpret since the number of plotted events can be difficult to discern. I suggest putting the event number on the plots. Also, on these plots, is it possible (was it done?) to isolate duplications that arose in that individual separately from those in the parental lineage? I understand that information may not always be available in the absence of multi-generational studies.
6) It’s a small detail, but I don’t think the authors should use the same red and green coloring for the traces and the arrows in figures like Fig. 3F. I don’t think they intend for the arrow colors to match the trace colors.
7) I especially like Fig. 5A, which does an excellent job placing the current observations in the context of tandem duplications in human cancer.

### Reviewer 3

In this manuscript, the authors reported that the tsk mutants rapidly accumulate large, heritable tandem duplications, which may be mediated by Pol θ. 1. The authors concluded that the tandem duplications in the tsk mutant were attributed to Pol θ, which was supported by the mutational signatures of the tandem duplications. Since this is one of the major findings of the manuscript, the genetic evidence is needed to further support it. As the tsk-4 teb-5 double mutant was lethal, the authors may consider to use the weak teb allele teb-3 (SALK_001669) or knock down TEB using RNAi. The lethality of tsk-4 teb-5 actually suggests that TSK and TEB can function independently. Given that the authors found that c-NHEJ was not responsible for the tandem duplications in tsk-4 mutants, it is possible that the HR pathway may be involved in this process. Therefore, it is worthwhile to cross tsk-4 with HR mutants such as brca1 and rad51 and test the phenotype of the double mutant.
2. They performed reciprocal crosses between the tsk-4 mutant and Col-0 and concluded that the developmental phenotypes of tsk-4 plants are associated with the absence of TSK rather than the presence of tandem duplications within the genome. Therefore, on the one hand, the authors need to increase the sample size. On the other hand, the authors need to examine the number of tandem duplications in TSK +/+, TSK +/-, and TSK -/- in the segregating population.

Some unknown factors may account for the enhanced tandem duplications in tsk-4. If the authors want to conclude that tandem duplications are induced by replication stress, they may examine tandem duplications in Col-0 and tsk-4 treated by replication stress-inducing chemicals such as hydroxyurea.
5. Statistical analysis is needed for Figures 2B, 2C, 2G, and 4D to test whether the difference is significant or not.

## Authors' Response to Round 1

We want to thank the reviewers for the comments provided on our initial manuscript. A point-by-point response to all comments is provided below.

We have also added new data in the revised manuscript that was not suggested by the reviewers, but that we believe is very important to our study based on questions we received when presenting this work. These experiments were initiated last summer and provided results after the initial submission of our manuscript to Nature Communications.

In the course of this study, we came to the conclusion that the copy number variations (CNVs) we were observing in tsk-4 mutant plants were tandem duplications. This was on account of chimeric short (150bp) reads being found linking the beginning and end of the CNV indicative of a breakpoint junction. Additionally, as shown in Figure S1E, these CNVs occurred at levels 1.5-2x the genomic DNA content of the wild type, suggesting a doubling of DNA.

However, mammalian cells experiencing various forms of genome instability have been shown to produce circular extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA), which are structures not integrated into chromosomes. Importantly, such structures are indistinguishable from tandem duplications in high-throughput short-read sequencing data. Therefore, there was a possibility that the CNVs identified in our study could be circular ecDNA.

Confirming a tandem duplication requires the identification of long DNA molecules that span the amplification itself and both junctions between amplified and non-amplified genomic DNA. To do this, we have now performed Optical Genome Mapping of a sample of pooled tsk-4 sibling plants and compared the resulting DNA molecules to 11 CNVs observed in the parent plant. We observed DNA molecules covering both copies of the duplication as well as flanking sequences for all CNVs up to 178 kb in size (6 CNVs), thus demonstrating that they are tandem duplications. While definitive results for the remaining larger CNVs were limited by the technical constraints of the assay, long DNA molecules consistent with tandem duplications were also found for all the remaining CNVs. Together, this new data confirms the conclusion that we are observing tandem duplications integrated into the chromosome of tsk-4 plants and not ecDNA. We included this data in the revised manuscript in Fig. 2.

We want to thank the reviewers for the comments provided on our initial manuscript. A point-by-point response to all comments is provided below.

We have also added new data in the revised manuscript that was not suggested by the reviewers, but that we believe is very important to our study based on questions we received when presenting this work. In the course of this study, we came to the conclusion that the copy number variations (CNVs) we were observing in tsk-4 mutant plants were tandem duplications. This was on account of chimeric short (150bp) reads being found linking the beginning and end of the CNV indicative of a breakpoint junction. Additionally, as shown in Figure S1E, these CNVs occurred at levels 1.5-2x the genomic DNA content of the wild type, suggesting a doubling of DNA.

However, mammalian cells experiencing various forms of genome instability have been shown to produce circular extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA), which are structures not integrated into chromosomes. Importantly, such structures are indistinguishable from tandem duplications in high-throughput short-read sequencing data. Therefore, there was a possibility that the CNVs identified in our study could be circular ecDNA.

Confirming a tandem duplication requires the identification of long DNA molecules that span the amplification itself and both junctions between amplified and non-amplified genomic DNA. To do this, we have now performed Optical Genome Mapping of a sample of pooled tsk-4 sibling plants and compared the resulting DNA molecules to 11 CNVs observed in the parent plant. We observed DNA molecules covering both copies of the duplication as well as flanking sequences for all CNVs up to 178 kb in size (6 CNVs), thus demonstrating that they are tandem duplications. While definitive results for the remaining larger CNVs were limited by the technical constraints of the assay, long DNA molecules consistent with tandem duplications were also found for all the remaining CNVs. Together, this new data confirms the conclusion that we are observing tandem duplications integrated into the chromosome of tsk-4 plants and not ecDNA. We included this data in the revised manuscript in Fig. 2.

They performed reciprocal crosses between the tsk-4 mutant and Col-0 and concluded that the developmental phenotypes of tsk-4 plants are associated with the absence of TSK rather than the presence of tandem duplications within the genome. But the evidence to support this conclusion is not strong. Based on Figure 4B, compared with TSK +/+ plants, many more TSK +/- plants showed a high percentage of nodes with double siliques (>25%), especially in tsk-4 x Col-0. The statistical insignificance of the difference between TSK +/- and TSK -/- may be due to the small sample size. It is still possible that the tandem duplications cause the developmental phenotypes. Therefore, on the one hand, the authors need to increase the sample size. On the other hand, the authors need to examine the number of tandem duplications in TSK +/+, TSK +/-, and TSK -/- in the segregating population.

We would like to point out that Fig. 4B represents the phenotyping of 244 plants, which is a large sample size when the data is collected by hand. Increasing the sample size will increase the statistical power to detect smaller effect sizes. Given that there is a detectable effect at this sample size, it is unlikely to change as the sample size increases.

We could examine the number of tandem duplications in the TSK +/+, TSK +/-, and TSK -/- population. However, as we showed that the tandem duplications occur throughout the genome and that they can be inherited (Fig. 3A-C), we expect no difference in the complements of tandem duplications between TSK +/+, TSK +/-, and TSK -/- genotypes.

Most importantly, consistent with the conclusion that we drew from this experiment is the work of Ohno et al. (2011, PMID: 21705754), and very recently Li et al. (2025, PMID: 41406205), which report that when tsk-4 plants were transformed with a pTSK::TSK-GFP or 35S::TSK-GFP transgene, the developmental phenotypes were fully complemented. The Li et al. study even performed the same double silique assay as our study. These results using an alternative method confirm our conclusion that lack of TSK activity causes the tsk-4 phenotypes, not the presence of tandem duplications.

Finally, our results demonstrating that loss of ATR (see below) or WEE1 strongly rescues the developmental phenotypes of tsk-4 also support that it is the absence of TSK which is responsible for the phenotypes (Fig. 5F-G), as we showed that inactivating WEE1 activity in tsk-4 mutants does not eliminate tandem duplications (Fig. 5D).

3. It was very interesting that wee1 and sog1 partially suppressed the developmental phenotypes of tsk-4. The authors mentioned that “The inability to repair damaged DNA in the absence of TSK is a source of cellular stress” (line 270). Given that WEE1 and SOG1 positively regulate DNA repair, it is likely that tsk wee1 and tsk sog1 accumulate more DNA damage, which needs to be tested. Alternatively, the phenotypes of tsk-4 are not due to DNA damage per se but due to the activation of DDR, which is suppressed when WEE1 or SOG1 is mutated. WEE1 and SOG1 are known to function downstream of ATR. Given the difference of wee1 and sog1 in suppressing tsk-4, it will be interesting to test whether atr can suppress tsk-4 better than wee1 and sog1.

WEE1 and SOG1 both positively regulate DNA repair, so we agree that additional DNA damage may be observed in tsk-4 wee1 and tsk-4 sog1 double mutants. However, we consider it unlikely that increased DNA damage, if present, is responsible for the observed suppression of developmental phenotypes. Endogenous DNA damage levels in tsk-4 are already very high, frequently sufficient to trigger cell death (Suzuki et al, 2003, PMID: 15125773). If this existing DNA damage (i.e., tandem duplications) does not drive the developmental defects (see reply to point 2), further impairment of DNA repair would, if anything, be expected to exacerbate, rather than suppress, these phenotypes. The observed phenotypic suppression therefore argues against a simple DNA-damage–driven mechanism.

We favor the explanation that the tsk-4 developmental phenotypes primarily reflect activation of replication-associated DDR signaling. WEE1 and SOG1 function not only in DNA repair, but also as key cell-cycle checkpoint effectors, regulating cell-cycle arrest, differentiation, and stem-cell fate decisions in response to genotoxic stress (De Schutter et al., 2007; PMID: 17209125; Cools et al., 2011; PMID: 21498679; Ogita et al., 2018; PMID: 29430765). We therefore propose that loss of WEE1 or SOG1 suppresses tsk-4 phenotypes mainly by attenuating checkpoint-mediated developmental responses, rather than by altering the underlying level of DNA damage. Consistent with this interpretation, we find that tandem duplications—the primary genomic instability phenotype analyzed in this study—continue to arise in tsk-4 wee1 and tsk-4 sog1 double mutants at comparable frequency and size to those observed in tsk-4 single mutants. To clarify this point, we have added the number of tandem duplications alongside Fig. 5D in the revised manuscript.

While interesting, we also believe that the manner in which the loss of WEE1 or SOG1 may alter the complex mutational profiles (i.e., indels, substitutions, structural variations, etc….) of the double mutants is outside the scope of this study for the practical reason of sample size (discussed in point 5 below).

Since our initial submission, we finalized the generation and phenotypic analyses of tsk-4 atr double mutant lines. We found that atr mutation indeed does suppress the tsk-4 developmental phenotypes even better than wee1. These new data provide strong genetic support that replication-associated ATR-dependent DDR signaling is the primary driver of the tsk-4 developmental defects. The new results on the analysis of tsk-4 atr-2 double mutants are presented below, and in Fig. 5F and Supp. Fig. S5 in the revised manuscript.

If the authors want to conclude that tandem duplications are induced by replication stress, they may examine tandem duplications in Col-0 and tsk-4 treated by replication stress-inducing chemicals such as hydroxyurea.
